newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - New NZ power mkt risks too much - Comalco.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - New NZ power mkt risks too much - Comalco.

text.p: New Zealand risks unfettered power price increases when it throws the switch on its new wholesale electricity market next month, aluminium producer Comalco New Zealand Ltd warned on Friday.
Managing director Kerry McDonald said the new market, which will become fully operational on October 1, was unbalanced in favour of power generators and seriously flawed.

"There are serious problems with it. It has the potential to damage our (Comalco's) position, it has the potential to damage the position of all of the consumers in New Zealand," McDonald told Reuters in an interview.
Comalco NZ, a unit of Australia's Comalco Ltd and New Zealand's largest consumer of electricity, resigned from the New Zealand Electricity Market (NZEM) on Thursday.
"A key issue with our resignation is we're putting up our hand and saying very clearly: 'look, this is going down an unsatisfactory path'," McDonald said.

"It's very important that consumers generally become quite strongly focussed on the issue, because otherwise they're going to wake up one morning and find their power bills are a hell of a lot higher than they were expecting."
He said there were "significant risks" of electricity prices rising and consumers being unable to do anything about it.
"And there's a signficant risk that at some time in the future, the market may be manipulated," he said.

Developing competition between all electricity market participants is at the heart of the new market. In contrast to the cost-based methods of the past, prices are to be discovered on the basis of the equilibrium between supply and demand.

But electricity purchaser and consumer groups have voiced concerns that the proposed market rules will allow the two state-owned generators, Contact Energy and Electricity Corp of New Zealand (ECNZ), to act unilaterally to push market prices above a competitive level, otherwise known as gaming.

"I am not saying that ECNZ (the largest generator of electricity in New Zealand) is going to game the market or use its dominant position, but the market should not be set up so that there is the opportunity for that," McDonald said.
He said the development of the market rules had left the structure "quite unbalanced".

"What you want is a market in which buyers and sellers can interact in a very even-handed way -- neither side can dominate. If there's potential to undermine or influence the market, then it should be roughly balanced between either side.

"What you've got now is a situation in which consumers fulfill a relatively weak role in the market. They are bidding in quantity and those quantities are aggregated, so no individual consumer really has an influence on the overall picture. It really is as simple as that."
McDonald slammed the market's structure, saying it was not conducive to efficiency.
"Because of the complexity and the cost structure of the market, I don't believe that there are adequate incentives on the market to reduce its costs and operate efficiently."
He said it was possible that other market participants would follow Comalco's lead in resigning from NZEM, but stressed that Comalco did not want to see the new market fail.

"What I want to see is changes to the constitution and processes of the market, so that we can influence change towards a more efficient market, rather than seeing a whole range of people pull away from it."

Earlier this month, the anti-monopolies Commerce Commission said it had no jurisdiction to pass judgement over the proposed market rules, which market operator EMCO (Electricity Market Company) had submitted for authorisation.
However, the monopolies watchdog said it did not believe the rules would lessen competition.
